Lessons.Title: Situations and Sequence Types
ExplanationParagraphs: Create and compare sequence equations from tables, growth percentages and context patterns.

For geometric sequence 16,24,36,54,81, each term is 1.5 times the previous, corresponding to 50 percent growth per step. A comparison of two population models requires calculating from each table and evaluating the same term index. Square-grid patterns can grow as arithmetic for their borders and quadratically for their interiors, so do not force an exponential model onto every growing picture. For f(0)=3 and f(n)=2f(n-1), f(n)=3*2^n.

Activity 10.1: Describing Growth: math source context — Here is a geometric sequence. What is the growth factor? 16, 24, 36, 54, 81 One way to describe its growth is to say it’s growing by \(\underline{\hspace{.25in}}\)% each time. What number goes in the blank for the sequence 16, 24, 36, 54, 81? Be prepared to explain your reasoning.. Work the source task, document quantities and justify the rule. Teacher checks any diagram, model or partner discussion.

Activity 10.2: Finding Population Patterns: math source context — The table shows two animal populations growing over time. Are the sequences represented by Population \(A\) and Population \(B\) arithmetic or geometric? Explain how you know. Write an equation to define Population \(A\). Write an equation to define Population \(B\). Does Population \(B\) ever overtake Population. Work the source task, document quantities and justify the rule. Teacher checks any diagram, model or partner discussion.

Activity 10.3: Finding Square Patterns: math source context — Define the sequence \(W\) so that \(W(n)\) is the number of white squares in Step \(n\), and define the sequence \(B\) so that \(B(n)\) is the number of black squares in Step \(n\). Are the sequences \(W\) and \(B\) arithmetic, geometric, or neither? Explain how you know. Write an equation for sequence \(W\). Write an. Work the source task, document quantities and justify the rule. Teacher checks any diagram, model or partner discussion.

Cumulative Problem 1: source mathematics — A sequence is defined by \(f(0) = 3, f(n) = 2 \boldcdot f(n-1)\) for \(n\ge1\). Write a definition for the \(n^{\text{th}}\) term of \(f\).. Preserve original index, signs, ratios and units; independent first-party answer and reasoning required.

Cumulative Problem 2: source mathematics — A geometric sequence, \(g(n)\) starts 20, 60, . . . Define \(g\) recursively and for the \(n^{\text{th}}\) term.. Preserve original index, signs, ratios and units; independent first-party answer and reasoning required.

Cumulative Problem 3: source mathematics — A geometric sequence \(g\) starts at 500 and has a growth factor of 0.6. Sketch a graph of \(g\) showing the first 5 terms.. Preserve original index, signs, ratios and units; independent first-party answer and reasoning required.

Cumulative Problem 4: source mathematics — An arithmetic sequence has \(a(1)=4\) and \(a(2)=16\). Explain or show how to find the value of \(a(15)\) A geometric sequence has \(g(0)=4\) and \(g(1)=16\). Explain or show how to find the value of \(g(15)\).. Preserve original index, signs, ratios and units; independent first-party answer and reasoning required.

Cumulative Problem 5: source mathematics — A piece of paper has an area of 96 square inches. Complete the table with the area of the piece of paper \(A(n)\), in square inches, after it is folded in half \(n\) times. Define \(A\) for the \(n^{\text{th}}\) term. What is a reasonable domain for the function \(A\)? Explain. Preserve original index, signs, ratios and units; independent first-party answer and reasoning required.

Cumulative Problem 6: source mathematics — Here is a growing pattern: Describe how the number of dots increases from Stage 1 to Stage 3. Write a definition for sequence \(D\), so that \(D(n)\) is the number of dots in Stage \(n\). Is \(D\) a geometric sequence, an arithmetic sequence, or neither? Explain how you know.. Preserve original index, signs, ratios and units; independent first-party answer and reasoning required.

Cumulative Problem 7: source mathematics — A paper clip weighs 0.5 grams and an empty envelope weighs 6.75 grams. Han adds paper clips one at a time to an empty envelope. Complete the table with the weight of the envelope \(w(n)\), in grams, after \(n\) paper clips have been added. Does \(w(10.25)\) make sense? Explain. Preserve original index, signs, ratios and units; independent first-party answer and reasoning required.

First-party independent cool-down: A geometric sequence starts 8,12,18. Find its growth factor and percentage increase, write an nth-term rule beginning at n=1 and find term five. Answer key: r=1.5, growth 50%; a(n)=8*(1.5)^(n-1); a(5)=40.5.

Assessment boundary: digital exact numeric questions may reuse an existing compatible family only if semantics match; diagrams, card discussion and written justifications require teacher verification. Source activities are guidance, not proof an interactive simulator exists.

KeyConcepts.Title: Percent growth factor
KeyConcepts.Definition: A multiplier r=1+p/100 corresponds to p percent growth.

KeyConcepts.Title: Equation from a sequence
KeyConcepts.Definition: Write a rule for any permitted term index.
KeyConcepts.Rule: f(n)=f(0)*r^n for geometric n starting at zero.

KeyConcepts.Title: Compare types
KeyConcepts.Definition: Check additive differences and multiplicative ratios.
KeyConcepts.Rule: An arithmetic border may coexist with quadratic interior.

WorkedExamples.Title: Growth percent
WorkedExamples.Question: The sequence 16,24,36,54,81 has what growth percent per step?
WorkedExamples.Method: Find the multiplier from two consecutive terms.

WorkedExamples.Title: Recursive to explicit
WorkedExamples.Question: f(0)=3 and f(n)=2f(n-1) for n>=1. Find f(5).
Steps: Five multiplications by two after n=0.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Treating a sequence rule as context-free.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: It can alter the index, initial term, units or learning target.
CommonMistakes.Correction: State the beginning term, domain and original lesson model.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Using a fixed common difference when the sequence is not arithmetic.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Differing consecutive differences invalidate the arithmetic formula.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Calculate two or more differences or ratios before selecting a rule.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Auto-grading graphs, card exchanges or manipulative proof from a number alone.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Numeric equality does not establish a correct diagram or explanation.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Use a teacher rubric for visual and reasoning evidence.
